questions.q: List the four main supporting characters in "The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse" and state one defining trait for each, based solely on your memory of the story.
questions.a: The four main supporting characters are: Mourad (impulsive yet honorable), Uncle Khosrove (irritable yet deeply homesick), John Byro (patient and trusting), and Zorab (practical and grounded). A wrong answer that lists Aram as a supporting character reveals confusion between protagonist and supporting roles. A wrong answer that assigns traits like "greedy" to Mourad or "vengeful" to John Byro reveals a failure to grasp the story's moral framework where the Garoghlanian code of honesty governs all actions.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Mourad insists "it wasn't stealing" when he takes the horse, and how this reflects the Garoghlanian tribe's unique moral code.
questions.a: Mourad distinguishes between stealing for profit (selling the horse) and stealing for the pure joy of riding, arguing that the latter isn't truly stealing because they never intend to deprive the owner permanently or gain materially. This reflects the tribe's code where intent and honor matter more than legalistic definitions — they are "proud first, honest next." A wrong answer that calls Mourad a hypocrite or thief misses the cultural nuance that the tribe's eleven-century reputation for honesty is maintained precisely because they draw this ethical line, and Mourad ultimately returns the horse unharmed and improved.

questions.q: Using the "STEAL" method (Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks), analyze Uncle Khosrove's character in the scene where John Byro reports his stolen horse. Provide one textual example for each element.
questions.a: Speech: "It is no harm; pay no attention to it" (repeated roars). Thoughts: Implied by his dismissal of material loss compared to loss of homeland. Effect on others: John Byro leaves frustrated; Aram's mother explains he has a "gentle heart" beneath the bluster. Actions: Slams the screen door and stalks out. Looks: "Enormous man with a powerful head of black hair and the largest moustache in the San Joaquin Valley." A wrong answer that only lists his anger without the homesickness context reveals a superficial reading that mistakes his bluster for his true character.

questions.q: Compare and contrast Mourad's and John Byro's relationships with the white horse. How do their differing interactions with the horse reveal their respective worldviews?
questions.a: Mourad relates to the horse as a kindred spirit — he sings to it, understands its wildness ("I have a way with a horse"), and rides it for ecstatic freedom. John Byro relates to the horse as a livelihood — he values it for the surrey, notices its improved condition ("stronger than ever, better-tempered"), and ultimately trusts the boys' honesty over his own eyes. Mourad's worldview is spiritual/experiential; Byro's is practical/relational. A wrong answer that says both love the horse equally misses the class/cultural divide: Mourad rides for transcendence, Byro needs the horse for survival.

questions.q: Evaluate the narrative decision to have John Byro say "Tooth for tooth... I would swear it is my horse if I didn't know your parents. The fame of your family for honesty is well known to me." Is this moment more about plot resolution or thematic reinforcement? Justify your answer.
questions.a: This moment is primarily thematic reinforcement. While it enables the plot resolution (the boys return the horse next morning), its deeper function is to validate the Garoghlanian code as a living social currency — Byro's willingness to distrust his own eyes because of the family's reputation proves that eleven centuries of honesty have tangible power. The phrase "A suspicious man would believe his eyes instead of his heart" elevates the theme: integrity creates its own reality. A wrong answer that calls it merely a plot device to avoid confrontation ignores how the story uses this exchange to show that honesty is not just personal virtue but communal capital.

questions.q: Create a diary entry from Zorab's (Mourad's father) perspective on the morning he discovers the horse is gone, revealing his practical nature and his complex relationship with his "crazy" son. Use at least two textual details about Zorab from the story.
questions.a: A strong entry would show Zorab's practicality (he is "practical and nothing else"), his awareness of the tribe's spirit distribution ("A man could be the father of his son's flesh, but that did not mean that he was also the father of his spirit"), and his likely quiet resignation rather than outrage. It might reference the deserted vineyard barn or the early morning rides. A poor entry would make Zorab angry or complicit, contradicting the text's explicit contrast between Zorab's practicality and Mourad's inheritance of Uncle Khosrove's "crazy streak."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of supporting characters involves examining the personality traits, motivations, ______, and narrative functions of characters who are not the protagonist, using textual evidence such as dialogue, actions, and authorial description to understand how they advance the plot, develop themes, and illuminate the protagonist's journey.
Fill in the blank: ______ you are watching a film where the hero's cousin steals a horse — you'd naturally ask: "Why does the cousin do it?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently identify all supporting characters in the story, cite specific textual evidence for each character's key traits, explain how each character's actions influence the plot and themes, and compare/contrast supporting characters with the protagonist to reveal deeper thematic insights.
